topics.title: Introduction and Applicability of AS 28
explain: AS 28 ensures that an enterprise's assets are carried at an amount not exceeding their recoverable amount.
It was made mandatory from 1 April 2004 for listed enterprises and entities with turnover exceeding ₹50 crores.
For all other commercial, industrial, and business reporting entities, it became mandatory from 1 April 2005.
If carrying amount exceeds recoverable amount, the asset is impaired and loss must be recognized in Profit and Loss.
topics.example: A company with a turnover of ₹60 crores in 2004 must mandatorily comply with AS 28 for accounting periods starting on or after 1-4-2004.
remember: Effective 1-4-2004 for Level 1 / turnover > ₹50 cr; 1-4-2005 for all others.
mistakes: Assuming AS 28 became mandatory for all entities at the same time in 2004.

quiz.q: From which date did AS 28 become mandatory for unlisted enterprises with turnover exceeding ₹50 crores?
quiz.why: AS 28 became mandatory from 1-4-2004 for listed entities and enterprises with turnover exceeding ₹50 crores.

quiz.q: What is the core objective of AS 28?
o: To revalue assets to market value
To ensure assets are not carried above recoverable amount
quiz.why: AS 28 ensures assets are carried at no more than their recoverable amount.

topics.title: Scope of AS 28 and Indicators of Impairment
explain: AS 28 applies to all assets EXCEPT inventories (AS 2), construction contract assets (AS 7), financial assets (AS 13), and deferred tax assets (AS 22).
An enterprise must assess at each balance sheet date whether any indication of impairment exists.
External indications include decline in market value, adverse technological/legal changes, rise in interest rates, or market cap dropping below net assets.
Internal indications include obsolescence, physical damage, plans to discontinue/restructure, or worse economic performance than expected.
topics.example: A factory machine suffers physical damage during a storm; this is an internal indication of impairment requiring an estimate of recoverable amount.
remember: AS 28 excludes Inventories (AS 2), Construction Contracts (AS 7), Financial Assets (AS 13), and Deferred Tax Assets (AS 22).
mistakes: Applying AS 28 rules to calculate impairment of inventory or deferred tax assets.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an EXCLUDED asset under AS 28?
quiz.why: AS 28 explicitly excludes inventories, construction contract assets, financial assets, and deferred tax assets.

quiz.q: Which of the following is considered an INTERNAL source of impairment indication?
o: Decline in market capitalization below net asset value
Evidence of physical damage or obsolescence
quiz.why: Obsolescence or physical damage comes from inside the business, making it an internal indicator.

topics.title: Measurement of Recoverable Amount
explain: Impairment Loss is the amount by which carrying amount exceeds recoverable amount.
Recoverable Amount is the HIGHER of Net Selling Price and Value in Use.
Net Selling Price is arm's length sale price less direct incremental disposal costs (excluding finance costs and tax).
Value in Use is the present value of estimated future cash flows expected from continuing use and disposal of the asset.
If either Net Selling Price or Value in Use exceeds Carrying Amount, the asset is not impaired.

flow.title: Determining Recoverable Amount
steps: Compare Net Selling Price and Value in Use

topics.example: A machine has Carrying Amount ₹100 lakhs, Net Selling Price ₹80 lakhs, and Value in Use ₹90 lakhs. Recoverable Amount is ₹90 lakhs (higher of 80 and 90). Impairment Loss = ₹10 lakhs.
remember: Recoverable Amount = HIGHER of Net Selling Price and Value in Use.
mistakes: Taking the lower of Net Selling Price and Value in Use to calculate recoverable amount.

quiz.q: Recoverable amount of an asset is defined as:
o: Lower of Net Selling Price and Value in Use
Higher of Net Selling Price and Value in Use
Sum of Net Selling Price and Value in Use
Average of Net Selling Price and Value in Use
quiz.why: Recoverable amount is the higher of net selling price and value in use.

quiz.q: Costs of disposal directly exclude which of the following expenses?
o: Finance costs and income tax expense
quiz.why: Costs of disposal exclude finance costs and income tax expenses.

topics.title: Basis and Composition of Future Cash Flows
explain: Cash flow projections should be based on management's recent approved budgets for a maximum of 5 years.
Projections beyond 5 years should extrapolate using a steady or declining growth rate based on long-term average rates.
Estimates include inflows from continuing use, directly attributable necessary outflows, and net cash flow on ultimate disposal.
Exclude cash flows from financing activities, income tax receipts/payments, uncommitted future restructurings, and capacity-enhancing capital expenditure.
Discount rate must be a pre-tax rate reflecting current market assessment of time value of money and specific asset risks.

flow.title: Estimating Value in Use Cash Flows
steps: Use Approved Budgets for Max 5 Years
Extrapolate Beyond 5 Years using Growth Rate
Include Inflows and Direct Operating Outflows
Exclude Financing, Tax, and Expansion Flows

topics.example: When calculating Value in Use of a truck, include fuel and maintenance outflows, but exclude interest paid on the loan taken to buy the truck.
remember: Maximum forecast period: 5 years. Discount rate: Pre-tax rate.
mistakes: Including interest costs or income tax payments in cash flow projections for Value in Use.

quiz.q: Under AS 28, financial budgets for cash flow projections should normally cover a maximum period of:
quiz.why: Cash flow projections are restricted to a maximum period of 5 years unless a longer period can be justified.

quiz.q: Which item SHOULD be included in future cash flow projections for Value in Use?
o: Directly attributable cash outflows from continuing use
Cash flows from future uncommitted restructurings
quiz.why: Directly attributable operating cash outflows necessary to generate inflows must be included.

topics.title: Recognition and Measurement of an Impairment Loss
explain: Impairment loss occurs when Carrying Amount > Recoverable Amount.
If asset is carried at cost, impairment loss is immediately charged as an expense to Profit & Loss Account.
If asset was previously revalued, impairment loss is first debited to Revaluation Surplus for that asset, and any remaining balance is charged to P&L.
After impairment recognition, future depreciation is recalculated on the revised carrying amount over remaining useful life.
If recoverable amount exceeds carrying amount, no loss is recognized, but depreciation parameters (useful life, method, residual value) should be reviewed under AS 10.

flow.title: Accounting for Impairment Loss
steps: Compare Carrying Amount with Recoverable Amount
If Yes, Debit Revaluation Surplus First

topics.example: Asset carrying value is ₹75 lakhs (includes ₹14 lakhs revaluation surplus). Recoverable amount is ₹12 lakhs. Loss = ₹15.30 lakhs. Charge ₹14 lakhs to Revaluation Reserve and ₹1.30 lakhs to P&L.
remember: Revalued Asset: Debit Revaluation Reserve up to existing surplus, balance to P&L.
mistakes: Writing off the entire impairment loss of a revalued asset to P&L without adjusting existing revaluation surplus.

quiz.q: How is impairment loss accounted for an asset carried at cost model?
o: Debited immediately to Profit & Loss Account
quiz.why: Impairment loss for an asset carried at cost is recognized as an expense in P&L immediately.

quiz.q: What happens to depreciation after an impairment loss is recognized?
o: Depreciation is recalculated on revised carrying amount
Depreciation is charged directly to reserve
quiz.why: Future depreciation is adjusted to allocate the revised carrying amount over the remaining useful life.

topics.title: Cash-Generating Units (CGU)
explain: A Cash-Generating Unit (CGU) is the smallest identifiable group of assets that generates cash inflows largely independent of other assets.
If recoverable amount cannot be determined for an individual asset, it must be determined for the CGU to which the asset belongs.
If an active market exists for output produced by an asset/group, it forms a separate CGU even if output is used internally.
Carrying amount of CGU includes carrying amounts of all assets, and liabilities if disposal of CGU requires buyer to take over the liability.

flow.title: Identifying and Testing a CGU
steps: Does asset generate independent cash inflows?
If No, identify smallest asset group (CGU)
Compare CGU Carrying Amount and Recoverable Amount

topics.example: A private railway owned by a mining company generates no independent cash flows. Recoverable amount is tested for the mine as a whole (the CGU).
remember: CGU = Smallest identifiable group generating independent cash inflows.
mistakes: Attempting to estimate Value in Use for an individual asset that cannot generate independent cash inflows.

quiz.q: A Cash-Generating Unit (CGU) is defined as:
o: The largest segment of a company
Smallest identifiable group of assets generating independent cash inflows
Any asset with a scrap value
quiz.why: AS 28 defines a CGU as the smallest group of assets generating largely independent cash inflows.

quiz.q: If a bus company operates 5 routes under one contract and cannot stop any single route, the CGU is:
o: The bus company as a whole
quiz.why: Since routes cannot be curtailed individually, cash inflows are independent only for all 5 routes together.

topics.title: Impairment of Goodwill
explain: Goodwill does not generate cash flows independently, so it must be tested for impairment as part of a CGU.
Bottom-Up Test: Used when goodwill can be allocated to CGUs on a reasonable and consistent basis.
Top-Down Test: Used when goodwill CANNOT be allocated reasonably; test CGU without goodwill first, then test smallest CGU including goodwill.
Impairment loss of a CGU is allocated FIRST to reduce goodwill to zero, and then to other assets of the unit pro-rata.

flow.title: Goodwill Impairment Testing Flow
steps: Can Goodwill be allocated to CGUs reasonably?
If Yes: Perform Bottom-Up Test only
If No: Perform Bottom-Up Test on CGUs first
Then perform Top-Down Test on larger unit
Allocate loss to Goodwill first, then pro-rata

topics.example: If a CGU suffers an impairment loss of ₹50 lakhs and has allocated goodwill of ₹30 lakhs, write off ₹30 lakhs from goodwill and remaining ₹20 lakhs pro-rata to other assets.
remember: Goodwill loss priority: First reduce Goodwill, balance allocated pro-rata to other CGU assets.
mistakes: Allocating impairment loss pro-rata to all CGU assets without fully writing off goodwill first.

quiz.q: When goodwill CANNOT be allocated to individual CGUs reasonably, which tests are performed?
quiz.why: If goodwill cannot be allocated reasonably, AS 28 requires performing both bottom-up and top-down tests.

quiz.q: In allocating impairment loss for a CGU, goodwill is written off:
o: After all fixed assets are written off
First, before allocating to other assets
Pro-rata along with all other assets
quiz.why: Impairment loss is allocated first to reduce goodwill of the CGU, then to other assets pro-rata.

topics.title: Corporate Assets and Allocation of Impairment Loss
explain: Corporate assets (e.g., HQ building, EDP equipment, R&D center) do not generate independent cash inflows.
If corporate assets can be allocated on a reasonable basis to a CGU, apply Bottom-Up test.
If corporate assets cannot be allocated on a reasonable basis, apply both Bottom-Up and Top-Down tests.
In allocating impairment loss, carrying amount of an asset cannot be reduced below HIGHEST of: (a) Net Selling Price, (b) Value in Use, and (c) Zero.
Any unallocated impairment loss is re-allocated pro-rata to other assets of the CGU.

flow.title: Allocating CGU Impairment Loss
steps: Allocate loss first to CGU Goodwill
Allocate remaining loss pro-rata to CGU assets
Check floor value for each asset
Floor = Max(Net Selling Price, Value in Use, 0)
Re-allocate excess loss to remaining assets

topics.example: A machine in an impaired CGU has a Net Selling Price of ₹15 lakhs. Its carrying value cannot be reduced below ₹15 lakhs during CGU impairment allocation.
remember: Asset floor limit in CGU allocation = Highest of Net Selling Price, Value in Use, or Zero.
mistakes: Reducing an individual asset's carrying value below its determinable net selling price during CGU impairment allocation.

quiz.q: Which of the following is classified as a corporate asset under AS 28?
quiz.why: Headquarters building, EDP equipment, and R&D centers are classic examples of corporate assets.

quiz.q: During CGU impairment allocation, an individual asset's carrying amount cannot be reduced below the highest of:
o: Net Selling Price, Value in Use, or Zero
Historical Cost, Book Value, or Scrap Value
Market Price, Salvage Value, or Residual Value
Fair Value, Cost of Goods Sold, or Zero
quiz.why: AS 28 specifies that an asset's carrying amount cannot be reduced below the highest of net selling price, value in use, and zero.

topics.title: Reversal of Impairment Loss
explain: Enterprise must assess at each balance sheet date if prior impairment loss has decreased or no longer exists.
If indications exist, estimate recoverable amount and reverse impairment loss.
Reversal is credited to P&L, or to Revaluation Surplus to the extent impairment was previously debited to Revaluation Surplus.
Increased carrying amount on reversal CANNOT exceed the carrying amount (net of depreciation) that would have been determined had no impairment occurred.
For a CGU, reversal is allocated pro-rata to non-goodwill assets first; Goodwill impairment CANNOT be reversed except under rare external events.

flow.title: Reversal of Impairment Loss
steps: Check Reversal Indications at Balance Sheet Date
Cap Carrying Value at Un-impaired Depreciated Value

topics.example: A machine impaired 2 years ago recovers in value. Its book value is ₹40 lakhs. Without past impairment, depreciated book value would be ₹60 lakhs. Reversal is capped to bring value up to ₹60 lakhs.
remember: Reversal Cap: Depreciated cost had no impairment occurred. Goodwill impairment reversal is generally PROHIBITED.
mistakes: Reversing goodwill impairment freely due to general economic recovery.

quiz.q: The revised carrying amount of an asset after reversing an impairment loss CANNOT exceed:
o: Carrying amount (net of depreciation) had no impairment been recognized
quiz.why: Reversal is capped at the carrying amount that would have been determined (net of depreciation) without prior impairment.

quiz.q: Can an impairment loss recognized for Goodwill be reversed in subsequent periods?
o: No, unless caused by a specific exceptional external event that reverses
quiz.why: AS 28 prohibits reversing goodwill impairment unless caused by a specific external event of exceptional nature that reverses.

topics.title: Impairment in Discontinuing Operations and Disclosures
explain: Approval and announcement of a plan for discontinuance is an indication of impairment.
If operation is sold substantially in its entirety, test the discontinuing operation as a whole CGU.
If operation is disposed via piecemeal sales or abandoned, test individual assets.
Disclosures required for each asset class: impairment losses recognized/reversed in P&L (and line items), and losses/reversals in revaluation surplus.
Disclose segment details (AS 17) and events/circumstances leading to material impairment loss or reversal.

flow.title: Discontinuing Operation Impairment
steps: If Yes, Test whole operation as CGU

topics.example: A company decides to close a division and sell machines one by one (piecemeal sale). Each machine is tested for impairment individually.
remember: Entirety sale = Test as one CGU; Piecemeal / Abandonment = Test individual assets.
mistakes: Ignoring impairment testing when a discontinuance plan is approved and announced.

quiz.q: If a discontinuing operation is disposed of through piecemeal sales, recoverable amount is estimated for:
o: The operation as a single CGU
quiz.why: For piecemeal sales, recoverable amount is determined for individual assets unless sold in groups.

quiz.q: AS 28 requires disclosure in financial statements for each class of assets regarding:
o: Impairment losses recognized/reversed in P&L and line items
quiz.why: AS 28 mandates disclosing the amount of impairment losses/reversals in P&L and the line items where they appear.
